exercises.name: Bench Press

steps: Before loading, have a qualified trainer check the rack, safety supports and spotter arrangement for this bench.
Lie with stable foot and bench contact and take a closed grip on the bar.
Lower the bar in a controlled path, then press it upward without bouncing.
Return the bar to its supports under control; rehearse the setup and return with a trainer before increasing load.
cues: Keep a closed grip on the bar.
Lower smoothly; do not bounce off the chest.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows out to 90 degrees puts unnecessary stress on the shoulder joint and reduces chest involvement.
Bouncing the bar off the chest instead of controlling the descent robs you of tension and increases injury risk.
Letting the hips or feet lift off the bench during the press also reduces stability and power transfer.
structured_content.benefits: Trains chest and arm strength with a supported barbell press.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Have a qualified trainer demonstrate the rack, spotter communication, and safety setup before loading the bar.

exercises.name: Incline Dumbbell Press

steps: Set an adjustable bench to a 30-45 degree incline and sit with a dumbbell in each hand resting on your thighs.
Kick the dumbbells up to shoulder height as you lie back, then press them up and slightly inward until your arms are extended above your upper chest.
Lower them with control back to just outside shoulder level before pressing again.
cues: Keep the dumbbells balanced above the forearms.
Maintain contact with the bench as you press.
mistakes: Setting the incline too steep (over 45-50 degrees) turns the movement into more of a shoulder press and takes emphasis off the chest.
Letting the dumbbells drift too far forward or crash together at the top reduces tension on the target muscles.
Arching the lower back excessively to move more weight is another common compensation to avoid.
structured_content.benefits: Trains chest and shoulder pressing strength on an inclined support.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Use a manageable pair and get help learning how to enter and leave the bench with the weights.

exercises.name: Push-Up

steps: Place the hands around shoulder width and support the body on hands and toes with the head aligned with the torso.
Bend the elbows to lower the body as a unit through a controlled range.
Push the floor away to return without letting the hips lag behind.
cues: Move the torso and hips together.
Keep the head aligned with the body.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor or piking them up removes tension from the target muscles and can strain the lower back.
Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides places excess stress on the shoulders.
Many people also only perform a partial range of motion, stopping well before the chest approaches the floor.
structured_content.benefits: Trains upper-body pushing strength while maintaining trunk control.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: If full push-ups are not controlled, ask a trainer to select a wall, stable elevated-support, or knee-supported variation. Those are different setups, not added weight on this record.

exercises.name: Chest Fly Machine

steps: Have staff adjust the seat, handles or forearm pads for your size according to the machine's instructions.
Take the handles with a comfortable elbow bend and keep that bend consistent as the arms move together.
Return under control through a comfortable range without letting the stack drop.
cues: Keep the elbow bend consistent through the arc.
Return the handles slowly without letting the stack slam.
mistakes: Using too much weight often causes people to turn the movement into a press by bending the elbows more and losing the arcing path.
Letting the handles snap back too quickly on the eccentric portion reduces muscle tension and increases strain on the shoulder joint.
Rounding the shoulders forward at the top of the squeeze can also place unwanted stress on the front of the shoulder.
structured_content.benefits: Trains bringing the upper arms together against machine resistance.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Ask staff to fit the seat and starting position to the specific machine before adding resistance.

exercises.name: Cable Crossover

steps: Set the two pulleys and attachments for the intended fly variation and choose manageable settings.
Take a stable stance and bring the handles together while keeping a small, consistent elbow bend.
Return the arms under control; keep the same chosen cable path rather than changing direction to move the load.
cues: Keep a small, consistent elbow bend.
Bring the handles together without rocking the torso.
mistakes: Changing the elbow bend to turn the fly into a press.
Rocking the torso to move resistance that cannot be controlled.
Switching the cable path mid-set instead of using the chosen variation consistently.

exercises.name: Overhead Press

steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, grip the barbell just outside shoulder width, and rest it on your front shoulders with elbows slightly in front of the bar.

Brace your core and glutes, then press the bar straight up, moving your head slightly back and then through once the bar clears your face, finishing with the bar directly over your ears and arms fully locked out.
Lower it back to the shoulders under control.
cues: Keep the wrists aligned with the forearms.
Avoid leaning back to finish the press.
mistakes: Leaning back excessively to help drive the bar up turns the lift into more of an incline press and stresses the lower back.
Failing to move the head out of the way results in a bar path that drifts forward instead of straight up, reducing efficiency and shoulder safety.
Not fully locking out the elbows or shrugging the shoulders up at the top also limits the strength benefit.
structured_content.benefits: Trains an overhead barbell press while stabilizing the trunk.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Learn the press and bar setup with a light implement before adding plates. Ask a trainer for an alternative if a comfortable overhead position is unavailable.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press

steps: Sit on a bench with back support, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height with palms facing forward.
Press both dumbbells straight up until your arms are fully extended, then lower them back to shoulder height under control.
Keep your core braced and avoid excessive arching of the lower back.
cues: Press both dumbbells without lifting off the back support.
Lower each weight with the same control.
mistakes: Letting the dumbbells drift too far forward changes the exercise into more of a front raise and reduces shoulder loading efficiency.
Overarching the lower back to gain leverage is a common compensation when the weight gets heavy.
Not lowering the dumbbells to a full shoulder-height stretch also shortchanges the range of motion.
structured_content.benefits: Trains overhead pressing with independently held dumbbells.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Use weights you can position and put down under control; ask for help learning the setup.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise

steps: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a slight bend in your elbows.
Raise both arms out to the sides until they reach roughly shoulder height, leading with your elbows rather than your hands, then lower them back down under control.
Avoid using momentum or swinging the torso to lift the weight.
cues: Raise the dumbbells without bouncing from the legs.
Keep a soft, consistent bend in the elbows.
mistakes: Swinging from the legs to start the raise.
Shrugging to move a load that cannot be raised with control.
Changing the elbow bend substantially between repetitions.
structured_content.benefits: Trains shoulder strength with a sideways arm raise.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Use a light pair and a range you can control without swinging.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Front Raise

steps: Hold one dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs with a stable stance.
Raise both arms together in front of the body through a controlled range without leaning back.
Lower both weights smoothly. Alternating and single-arm versions are separate variations.
cues: Raise both dumbbells together.
Keep the torso still as the weights return.
mistakes: Raising the dumbbells above shoulder height shifts stress toward the traps and reduces front delt tension.
Using body momentum by leaning back or swinging the arms up quickly is a very common compensation with heavier weights.
Because the front delts are already heavily worked by pressing exercises, overdoing this movement can also lead to unnecessary shoulder fatigue.
structured_content.benefits: Trains the front of the shoulders with a forward arm raise.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Use a light pair; keep both arms moving together for this bilateral record.

exercises.name: Reverse Fly

steps: Hinge forward at the hips with a slight bend in your knees, holding a dumbbell in each hand hanging below your shoulders with palms facing each other.
Keeping a slight bend in your elbows, raise both arms out to the sides in an arcing motion until they're roughly in line with your torso, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower back down under control.
cues: Open the arms without jerking the torso upward.
Keep the elbow bend consistent as the weights lower.
mistakes: Standing too upright rather than hinging forward reduces the effectiveness of the movement and shifts stress to the lower back.
Using momentum by jerking the weights up, or letting the elbows bend too much and turning it into a row, both reduce rear delt isolation.
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears at the top of the movement also pulls tension away from the target muscle.
structured_content.benefits: Trains the rear shoulders and upper back with a dumbbell fly.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: If holding the hinged position is difficult, ask about a chest-supported variation using an incline bench; it needs different equipment from this record.

exercises.name: Deadlift

steps: Have a trainer establish the stance, bar position, secure grip and bracing setup before adding load.
With the bar close and balanced foot pressure, extend the knees and hips to stand without jerking the bar.
Return the bar under control using the practiced hip and knee motion. Stop if the setup cannot be maintained.
cues: Keep the bar close during the lift.
Stand up without leaning back at the top.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back during the pull is the most serious technique error and significantly increases injury risk.
Letting the bar drift away from the shins and thighs during the lift makes it mechanically harder and puts more strain on the lower back.
Hyperextending (leaning back excessively) at the top of the lift is another common but unnecessary compensation.
structured_content.benefits: Trains a coordinated floor lift through hip and knee extension with trunk stabilization.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Learn the start position, grip, bracing and controlled return with qualified instruction before adding load.

exercises.name: Romanian Deadlift

steps: Stand holding a barbell at hip height with a shoulder-width grip.
Keeping your legs almost straight with just a slight knee bend, hinge at the hips and push your glutes backward, lowering the bar down the front of your legs while keeping your back flat.
Stop when you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings (typically around mid-shin), then drive your hips forward to return to standing.
cues: Send the hips back while the bar stays close.
Keep the chosen knee bend steady through the descent.
mistakes: Bending the knees too much turns the movement into more of a squat and reduces hamstring loading.
Rounding the back to reach further down is a common and risky compensation — the range of motion should be limited by hamstring flexibility, not by rounding the spine.
Letting the bar drift away from the legs also increases lower back stress.
structured_content.benefits: Trains hip-hinge strength with the bar starting from standing.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: First learn how to bring the bar to the standing start position and return it safely. Hinge only as far as you can maintain control.

exercises.name: Pull-Up

steps: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width, arms fully extended.
Pull your body up by driving your elbows down and back until your chin clears the bar, keeping your core engaged and avoiding excessive swinging.
Lower back down under control to a full arm extension before starting the next rep.
cues: Keep the body from swinging.
Lower under control instead of dropping.
mistakes: Using momentum by kipping or swinging the legs turns the exercise into a much less effective, less controlled movement for most training goals.
Not achieving a full range of motion — stopping short of chin-over-bar at the top or not fully extending the arms at the bottom — reduces the training effect.
Excessive shoulder shrugging without engaging the lats is another common inefficiency.
structured_content.benefits: Trains vertical pulling against bodyweight.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: If you cannot perform a controlled repetition, ask a trainer to select an appropriately supported or assisted alternative rather than forcing this unassisted movement.

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown

Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back, keeping a slight backward lean in your torso, then let it return under control to a full overhead stretch.
Avoid using your body weight to yank the bar down.
cues: Pull the elbows down without swinging backward.
Guide the bar back up without releasing control.
mistakes: Leaning back too far and using body momentum to heave the bar down reduces lat engagement and can strain the lower back.
Pulling the bar behind the neck rather than to the front of the chest places unnecessary and potentially risky stress on the shoulder joint.
Not allowing a full stretch at the top of each rep also limits the range of motion benefit.

structured_content.beginner_guidance: Have the thigh support and seat fitted before starting; use a resistance that lets you stay seated and control the return.

exercises.name: Seated Cable Row

steps: Sit at the cable row station with feet braced on the platform and knees slightly bent, gripping the handle with arms extended and torso upright.
Pull the handle toward your lower abdomen by driving your elbows straight back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then extend your arms back out under control without rounding your lower back.
cues: Pull without rocking the torso back.
Control the reach as the handle returns.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back or leaning too far forward and back (using body momentum rather than the arms and back) is the most common technique breakdown, especially as fatigue sets in.
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears reduces mid-back engagement.
Not pulling the handle far enough back to fully retract the shoulder blades also limits the benefit.

exercises.name: T-Bar Row

steps: Straddle the T-bar row landmine with feet shoulder-width apart, hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor, and grip the handles with a neutral or wide grip.
Pull the weight up toward your chest or upper abdomen by driving your elbows back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then lower under control to a full stretch.

Lower the plates without a sudden drop.
mistakes: Rounding the back during the pull, especially as the weight gets heavy, is the most significant risk with this exercise.
Standing too upright rather than maintaining a solid hip hinge reduces back engagement and shifts the movement pattern.
Using momentum by jerking the torso up and down instead of pulling with the back muscles is another common error.

exercises.name: Barbell Curl

steps: Stand holding a barbell with an underhand, shoulder-width grip, arms fully extended and elbows close to your torso.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows only, keeping your upper arms stationary, then lower it back down under control to full extension.
Avoid swinging your hips or back to help lift the weight.
cues: Keep the upper arms beside the torso.
Lower the bar without using a backward lean.
mistakes: Using momentum by swinging the torso back and forth (often called 'cheat curling') is extremely common once the weight gets challenging, and it significantly reduces the effectiveness of the exercise.
Letting the elbows drift forward away from the torso also changes the movement pattern and reduces bicep isolation.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom of each rep shortens the effective range of motion.
structured_content.benefits: Trains elbow flexion with a two-handed bar.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Start with a light bar you can control. An EZ-bar is a separate equipment choice; do not assume it weighs the same.

exercises.name: Preacher Curl

Grip the short bar with the palms up and curl while keeping the upper arms supported.

Lower the bar smoothly without bouncing at the bottom.

exercises.name: Tricep Pushdown

Push the attachment down by extending your elbows until your arms are fully straight, keeping your upper arms stationary, then let it return under control back to the starting position.

Return the attachment without letting the stack drop.

exercises.name: Skull Crushers

steps: Have a trainer demonstrate the bench setup, handling and return of the EZ-bar before adding load.
Lie supported on the bench and hold the EZ-bar securely above the upper body.
Bend and extend the elbows through a controlled range; stop before the bar becomes difficult to control.
Return the bar using the setup practiced with your trainer; do not improvise a failed-repetition bailout.
cues: Lower the EZ-bar deliberately.
Keep the grip secure throughout the return.
mistakes: Letting the upper arms drift backward or forward during the movement (rather than staying vertical) changes the exercise into something closer to a skull-crusher-pullover hybrid and reduces the intended muscle emphasis.
Using too much weight often leads to shortened range of motion or the elbows flaring out excessively.
Lowering the weight too far without control also increases the risk of hitting the head or straining the elbow.
structured_content.benefits: Trains elbow extension while lying on a bench with an EZ-bar.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Learn this setup with a qualified trainer. If you cannot control the load or it causes discomfort, stop and ask for a suitable alternative.

exercises.name: Parallel Bar Dip

steps: Grip parallel bars with arms extended and your body suspended above them, leaning your torso slightly forward.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor, then press back up to full arm extension.
Keep your core engaged and avoid excessive swinging.
cues: Keep the body from swinging between the bars.
Press back up without bouncing from the bottom.
mistakes: Descending too deep, especially with limited shoulder mobility, can place excessive strain on the front of the shoulder joint.
Flaring the elbows out wide rather than keeping them closer to the body increases shoulder stress.
Using momentum by bouncing at the bottom of the movement rather than controlling the descent also increases injury risk.
structured_content.benefits: Trains a compound bodyweight press using the chest, triceps and shoulders.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Ask a trainer to assess whether you can support and lower your body under control. Assisted alternatives need their own equipment and tracking.

exercises.name: Back Squat

steps: Have a trainer fit the rack and safety supports and teach the unrack, walkout and return before loading.
Support the bar on the upper-back position taught for the chosen squat variation, not on the neck.
Bend the hips and knees through a depth that allows stable balance and trunk control, then stand.
Return to the rack under control using the practiced sequence.
cues: Keep steady foot pressure as you descend.
Stand without letting the bar shift on the back.
mistakes: Letting the knees cave inward (valgus collapse) during the ascent is a common and potentially risky compensation, often linked to weak hip muscles or insufficient depth practice.
Rounding the lower back, especially at the bottom of a deep squat, increases injury risk.
Rising onto the toes or shifting weight forward due to poor ankle mobility also disrupts balance and bar path.
structured_content.benefits: Trains leg and hip strength with a back-supported barbell.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Learn the rack, walkout and return with a qualified trainer before loading; use a depth you can control.

exercises.name: Front Squat

steps: Have a trainer establish the front-rack grip and safety setup, with the bar supported on the front shoulders rather than held up by the hands.
With stable foot contact, bend the hips and knees through a depth that preserves the rack position and control.
Stand and return the bar to the rack using the practiced sequence.
cues: Keep the bar supported on the front of the shoulders.
Maintain the rack position while standing up.
mistakes: Letting the elbows drop during the squat causes the torso to lean forward and the bar to roll off the shoulders, which is the single most common technique breakdown.
Insufficient wrist or shoulder mobility often leads people to grip the bar in a way that strains the wrists rather than truly resting it on the shoulders.
Rushing depth without adequate ankle and hip mobility can also cause the heels to lift or the back to round.
structured_content.benefits: Trains leg strength while supporting a barbell in a front-rack position.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Have a trainer teach a comfortable front-rack setup and rack return before loading.

exercises.name: Leg Press

steps: Have staff adjust the seat and explain the start/stop mechanism of this selectorized leg press.
With the back and pelvis supported and feet securely on the platform, press through a controlled range.
Return without letting the pelvis lift off the pad or the stack drop.
Let the resistance settle and follow the machine's instructions before leaving the seat.
cues: Keep the pelvis supported through the repetition.
Return the platform under control.
mistakes: Losing pelvis or back contact with the support.
Letting the resistance return faster than it can be controlled.
Using a machine without first learning its adjustment and stopping mechanism.
structured_content.benefits: Trains leg pressing against a machine's resistance.
structured_content.beginner_guidance: Have staff demonstrate the seat, selector and start/stop mechanism on the actual machine.
